slides.heading: How Carbon Capture Technology Works
slides.body: The science pulling CO₂ out of the air — and why it might save us

slides.heading: The Core Problem
slides.body: CO₂ levels have surpassed 430 ppm — the highest in 3 million years. Even if we stopped all emissions today, existing atmospheric CO₂ would continue warming the planet for decades. Carbon capture aims to reverse this buildup.

slides.heading: Two Main Approaches
slides.body: Point-source capture grabs CO₂ directly from factory or power-plant exhaust before it reaches the air. Direct Air Capture (DAC) pulls CO₂ from the open atmosphere anywhere on Earth — far harder, but more flexible.

slides.heading: How DAC Actually Works
slides.body: Giant fans push air through chemical filters — either liquid solvents or solid sorbents — that bind CO₂ molecules. The material is then heated to release a pure CO₂ stream, regenerating the filter for reuse. It's essentially a giant artificial tree.

slides.heading: Storing the Carbon
slides.body: Captured CO₂ is compressed and injected deep underground into porous rock formations, often depleted oil and gas reservoirs. Mineralization turns it into solid carbonate rock within years — a permanent, geologically stable solution.

slides.heading: The Energy Challenge
slides.body: Today's DAC plants consume 1,500–2,000 kWh of energy per ton of CO₂ removed. If powered by fossil fuels, capture creates nearly as much CO₂ as it removes. Renewable energy integration is critical — and is driving massive innovation.

slides.heading: Current Scale & Cost
slides.body: The world's largest DAC facility, Mammoth in Iceland, captures 36,000 tons of CO₂ per year at roughly $1,000 per ton. Humanity emits ~37 billion tons annually. Costs must drop to under $100/ton to become climate-significant.

slides.heading: Nature-Based Carbon Capture
slides.body: Forests, wetlands, and oceans already capture ~11 billion tons of CO₂ per year. Enhanced approaches — afforestation, ocean iron fertilization, enhanced rock weathering — can amplify this at far lower cost than engineered solutions.

slides.heading: Who's Building It
slides.body: Climeworks, Carbon Engineering, and dozens of startups are racing to scale. Microsoft, Stripe, and Shopify have committed billions in advance purchase agreements. In 2026, the US Department of Energy funds 7 regional DAC hubs targeting 1 million tons/year.

slides.heading: The Road Ahead
slides.body: Carbon capture alone won't solve climate change — but it's a critical tool in the toolkit. As costs fall and scale grows, every ton removed buys time for deeper systemic change. The race to clean the air is just beginning.
